clue.text: O'Reilly's header follows short corner from England (5)

indicators.note: A header is the line printed at the top of a page, so what is wanted is the letter at the top of the name beside it.
Something cut short stops before its proper end, so the word loses its final letter.
What follows comes along afterwards, so this letter is written at the end rather than the front.

blocks.note: a corner is an angle, docked of its last letter
the letter O'Reilly starts with

explanation.surface: A player called O'Reilly heading in a corner that was taken short.
explanation.walkthrough: The football is the whole disguise: 'corner' is the geometry word rather than the set piece, and 'header' asks for a top letter rather than a goal.
explanation.definitionFit: Anglo is the adjective English speakers use for anything English in origin - Anglo-Irish, an Anglo abroad - so it stands for 'from England'.

clue.text: Republican wearing preposterous clobber in Senate for speech (5)

indicators.note: Clothes go round the person wearing them, so the letter named first is written inside the garment named next.
Preposterous is literally before-behind, so the word it marks is set down the other way round.

blocks.note: clobber is British slang for clothes and the Roman Senate wore togas, written here back to front
R after a name is how American reporting marks a Republican

explanation.surface: A Republican got up in ridiculous robes to address the Senate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Preposterous' is doing its literal Latin work, prae before and posterus behind, rather than merely calling the outfit silly. The Senate in the picture is Washington's; the one that supplies the garment is Rome's.
explanation.definitionFit: Argot is the private speech of a closed group - thieves' argot, a trade's argot - so it names a way of talking rather than an address.

clue.text: Hurried to visit holiday home in Rock (7)

indicators.note: A visitor spends the afternoon inside the house, so the word just named is written within the one that follows.

blocks.note: a gite is the French self-catering cottage the British rent by the week
someone who hurried ran

explanation.surface: Someone dashing off to stay in a rented cottage at Rock.
explanation.walkthrough: Rock is a Cornish seaside village stuffed with holiday homes, which is the picture the capital letter sells; the answer wants the mineral instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Granite is a rock, the hard speckled stone quarried in Cornwall and Aberdeen and cut for kerbs and headstones.

clue.text: Superior cakes start to leave one lad desperate for more (6)

indicators.note: Mud cakes a boot by covering it all over, so the word before this closes round what comes next.
The start of a word is the letter it opens with, and that is all this takes from the word after it.

blocks.note: a superior officer is the one over you
the opening letter of leave
one written as the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Expensive cakes being cleared away just as a hungry boy hoped for seconds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cakes' looks like the pastries on the plate and is a verb: to cake is to coat all over. The boy is Dickens's, holding out his bowl in the workhouse.
explanation.definitionFit: Oliver Twist is the workhouse boy who asks for more, the best-known hungry child in English fiction.

clue.text: Just over half of US adults currently back shelling Middle East (5)

definitions.text: Just over half of US adults

indicators.note: Sent back, a word in an across entry is read the other way along the row, last letter first.
A shell closes right round whatever is inside it, so the letters named next go within the word just turned.

blocks.note: what is happening currently is happening now, written backwards
ME is the newsroom's short form of the Middle East

explanation.surface: A poll finding a bare majority of American adults in favour of bombarding the Middle East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' is the pollster's verb, to support, and the instruction to reverse. The definition is a head-count rather than a synonym, which is why no dictionary would give it.
explanation.definitionFit: Women make up a little over half the adult population of the United States, so counting heads is the definition.

clue.text: Session band inspired by White and Plant (10)

indicators.note: To inspire is literally to breathe in, so the word doing the inspiring closes round the letters just named.

blocks.note: a wan face is a white one, drained of its colour
a school term is a session of teaching
ELO is the Electric Light Orchestra, the Birmingham band of the 1970s

explanation.surface: A studio band taking its lead from two famous rock musicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' is the definition and not Robert Plant, and 'White' wants the pale adjective rather than Jack. The pair of them read as a rock line-up, which is the whole disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: A watermelon grows on a trailing vine of the gourd family, so 'Plant' is the plainest category word available for it.

clue.text: Strike with backspin and kiss a red (4)

indicators.note: A ball struck with backspin comes back the way it went, so the word beside it is written in reverse.

blocks.note: to ram something is to strike it, and the spin turns the word round
the X at the foot of a letter is a kiss

explanation.surface: A snooker player striking with backspin to kiss a red.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is snooker, where a kiss is one ball brushing another and the reds are the balls worth a point. The definition wants the political colour instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A red is a communist, and Karl Marx is the man the whole tradition is named from, so he is the red by example.

clue.text: Number going topless to support Newton’s newspaper (8)

indicators.note: Going topless, a word loses what is on top, which in a down entry is its first letter.
In a down entry whatever supports something props it up from underneath, so these letters go below the one already given.

blocks.note: N is the symbol for the newton, the unit of force named after him
a rational number is one you can write as a fraction, here minus its first letter

explanation.surface: A model going topless to raise money for Newton's own paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' is the trap: it wants to be a quantity and it is the mathematician's rational. The National is Glasgow's pro-independence daily, which is how one word can define a whole title.
explanation.definitionFit: The National is the name of a Scottish daily paper, so the definition points at a particular masthead rather than at papers in general.

clue.text: One out of Vietnam, retired soldier no longer attached? (3)

definitions.text: One out of Vietnam, retired soldier no longer attached?

indicators.note: Taking one out of a thing leaves the remainder, so this letter is struck from the word beside it.
Somebody retired has turned back from the work, and a word that retires is set down the other way round.
What is no longer attached has come away altogether, so those letters are gone from what is left.

blocks.note: the country in full, seven letters, before two pieces are taken out of it
one written as the Roman numeral I, the first piece to go
a man is a soldier, and retired he is written backwards

explanation.surface: Somebody home from Vietnam and no longer serving with his unit.
explanation.walkthrough: Both deletions come out of the country's own name, which is how the sentence manages to describe the man and build him at the same time. 'Retired' is the about-turn, not the pension.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: an American vet is a veteran of Vietnam, a soldier out of the service and attached to no unit any more.

clue.text: People generally into Rivals? (7)

indicators.note: Going into a thing is going inside it, so the letters just named are written within the word that follows.

blocks.note: to vie is to compete, so viers are those who vie - rivals, a word that survives mainly in crosswords
we is how people in general speak of themselves

explanation.surface: The people who spend their evenings watching the television serial Rivals.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make Rivals a title, so the sentence is at once a description of the people watching it and the instruction that assembles them. Without the italics it would read as a taste for one's competitors.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: the people generally into a television serial are precisely the ones watching it, and Rivals is one such serial.

clue.text: Much-loved walk around historic city in Kent? (9)

indicators.note: What goes around a thing wraps right round it, so everything that follows is written inside this word.
A town in a county sits inside it, so these letters are placed within the two that stand for the county.

blocks.note: to tread is to walk, and the word opens up to take the rest inside
Kent is the county in the far south-east corner of England, SE on any address
Ur is the Sumerian city of the Old Testament and the crossword's standing answer for an ancient one

explanation.surface: A favourite walk that loops round an old cathedral city in Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: Kent sits in England's south-eastern corner, and the question mark admits that any of several counties would do as well. Ur, in what is now southern Iraq, is the ancient city every setter reaches for first.
explanation.definitionFit: Something treasured is held dear and kept safe, which is what calling a thing much-loved says about it.

clue.text: Giro d'Italia surprisingly drops all but one international combatant (9)

indicators.note: A surprising outcome is not the one you expected, so the letters do not stay in the order they were given.
Where the same letter turns up more than once, dropping all but one leaves a single copy standing.

blocks.note: the letters of the Italian race, eleven of them
international is I, and the three I's in the fodder come down to one

explanation.surface: The Giro d'Italia unexpectedly losing nearly all of its foreign riders.
explanation.walkthrough: The Giro d'Italia is Italy's three-week stage race, so the surface reads as a sports headline about riders pulling out. Nothing in it points anywhere near an arena.
explanation.definitionFit: A gladiator was the man sent into the Roman arena to fight, which is combatant in its oldest and most literal sense.

clue.text: Melody's unprotected sex with other folk (5)

indicators.note: Left unprotected, a word loses the letters standing guard at each end.

blocks.note: the people who are not us are them
SEX with its outer letters stripped off keeps only the middle one

explanation.surface: Melody sleeping around without taking precautions.
explanation.walkthrough: Melody reads as a girl's name and is the musical noun. The clue's least printable word is the one that gives up a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A theme is the tune a piece keeps returning to - a film's theme, a theme and variations - which is a melody under another name.

clue.text: Modernist who wrote revolutionary score for soap? (8)

indicators.note: A revolution turns a thing right round, so the name just given is written backwards.

blocks.note: T S Eliot is the modernist poet, turned round
a try is the score in rugby, worth five points

explanation.surface: A modernist writer's radical music for a television serial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soap' is the serial on the surface and the bar in the bathroom underneath. 'Score' is the rugby one, not the musical one the writer has set up.
explanation.definitionFit: Soap is the toiletry every bathroom holds, so the definition names one member of the class the answer covers, which is what the question mark admits.

clue.text: Rod’s making Penny jack in Michael McIntrye and co? (6)

indicators.note: On a price tag p is a penny and in a pack of cards J is the jack, and making the one into the other puts the J exactly where the P stood.

blocks.note: pokers are the iron rods kept beside a fire, one letter of which is about to be traded

explanation.surface: Rod talking Penny out of her fondness for Michael McIntyre and the other stand-ups.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack in' is British for giving a thing up, which is what holds the sentence together, while 'jack' alone is the card that does the work. Michael McIntyre is one of Britain's best-known stand-up comedians.
explanation.definitionFit: A joker is anyone who makes a living being funny, so a famous comedian and his rivals define the word by example.

clue.text: To Meloni, the Left say: “Reformation of Italy is wrong” (10)

indicators.note: A reformation makes a thing over in a new shape, so the word that follows is re-formed into a different order.

blocks.note: Giorgia Meloni is Italy's prime minister, and in her language 'the' is il
L is the standard short form of left
eg introduces an example, which is the job 'say' does in a sentence
the five letters of Italy in a new order

explanation.surface: The Italian left telling their prime minister that remaking the country is wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reformation' wants to be the historical event and is the instruction to re-form. The 'the' the clue asks for is the Italian one, which is what 'To Meloni' is there to tell you.
explanation.definitionFit: An illegality is a wrong in the legal sense, a thing done against the law, so noun answers noun.

clue.text: Hard-living thespian told to give up booze; ... (4)

indicators.note: To give a thing up is to let it go, so those letters leave the word standing before them.

blocks.note: a story told is a story reported
port is the fortified wine sent round the table after dinner

explanation.surface: A famously hard-drinking actor ordered off the drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliver Reed drank his way through two decades of chat shows, so the sentence reads as his own biography. The semicolon hands the thought on to the next clue, which is about the friend he drank with.
explanation.definitionFit: Oliver Reed was the British actor whose drinking became better known than his films, so 'hard-living thespian' names him by reputation.

clue.text: Fix up mushroom skewers in Asian wrap? (4,5)

indicators.note: In a down entry a word written up runs the other way, its last letter arriving first.
A skewer is pushed straight through the middle of what it holds, so the thing doing the skewering ends up inside.

blocks.note: to repair is to fix, and in a down entry 'up' stands the word on its head
a cep is the fat brown mushroom prized in French cooking

explanation.surface: A recipe telling you to sort out the mushroom skewers served in an Asian wrap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fix' is the mending sense, not pinning a mushroom in place. Rice paper is the translucent sheet dipped in water and rolled round the filling of a Vietnamese summer roll.
explanation.definitionFit: Rice paper is the edible sheet that goes round a Vietnamese summer roll, so it is literally a wrap from Asia.

clue.text: ... wild feller with no boundaries, Harris? (10)

definitions.text: wild feller with no boundaries, Harris?

indicators.note: Something wild will not keep to the order it was put in, so these letters come out rearranged.
The boundaries of a word are the letters at either end, and with those gone only the middle survives.

blocks.note: FELLER loses the letter at each end
six more letters for the mix, and the man being described

explanation.surface: An untamed fellow who respects no limits, Harris among them.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Harris drank and brawled his way through the 1960s alongside the actor at 14 across, so the sentence describes him twice over: once as a portrait, once as letters to be shaken up.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: a wild fellow who keeps to no limits is exactly what the word means, and Harris is the standing example of one.

clue.text: Quiet writer tense about working under old adversary (8)

indicators.note: A scarf worn about the neck goes right round it, so the word that follows is written inside the one before.
In a down entry what is under something sits below it, so the letter for old is written first and the rest beneath.

blocks.note: o. is the dictionary's short form for old
p for piano is the musician's mark for playing softly
the pen stands in for the writer holding it
a machine that is working is on
t. is the grammarian's short form for tense

explanation.surface: A shy author made nervous by having to work for an old enemy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tense' is the grammarian's word, not the mood the surface gives the writer. P for quiet is borrowed from music, where piano marks a passage to be played softly.
explanation.definitionFit: Your opponent is whoever is set against you in a game or an argument, which is what an adversary is.

clue.text: Did advocate impeach Don "incorrectly"? (10)

indicators.note: Done incorrectly, a thing comes out in the wrong order, which is what happens to these letters.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: Asking whether the lawyer went about impeaching Don the wrong way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Did advocate' is a past-tense verb, not the noun in the wig that the sentence wants. The quotation marks round the last word are the setter pointing at his own instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To champion a cause is to speak up for it in public, and the past tense matches 'did advocate' word for word.

clue.text: American buffoon claiming Greenland's core port ... (7)

indicators.note: A country claiming a territory takes it inside its own borders, so the letter named next goes within.
The core of a thing is its very middle, so this takes the single letter at the centre.

blocks.note: A is the dictionary label for American
the letter at the dead centre of GREENLAND
a twerp is a fool, British playground slang

explanation.surface: A clownish American laying claim to the middle of Greenland.
explanation.walkthrough: The American buffoon is the one who keeps announcing he wants Greenland, and the trailing dots carry him straight into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Antwerp is the Belgian seaport on the Scheldt, one of the busiest container ports in Europe.

clue.text: Romeo and Posh featured in Standard (4)

indicators.note: Whatever is featured in a paper appears inside it, so this letter is written within the letters that follow.

blocks.note: std is the everyday abbreviation of standard
U is the label for upper-class usage, from the old quarrel about U and non-U English

explanation.surface: Romeo and Posh Spice both getting a mention in the Evening Standard.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics turn Standard into a newspaper - London's Evening Standard - while the answer needs the plain adjective. Posh for U comes from the 1950s argument about which words were upper class.
explanation.definitionFit: A stud is a man with a reputation for conquests, which is what calling someone a Romeo means.

clue.text: ... opposes leaders in the hostile West after rebuking Trump so ... (7)

indicators.note: The leader of a word is the letter out in front of it, so this takes the front letter of every word that follows.

blocks.clueFragment: the hostile West after rebuking Trump so
blocks.note: the opening letter of each of the seven words in turn

explanation.surface: Western leaders standing up to a hostile power once they had told Trump off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaders' reads as heads of government, which is what the sentence is about, and asks for initials instead. Seven words in a row all pulling their weight is why the surface has to strain a little.
explanation.definitionFit: To thwart someone is to block what they were trying to do, which is opposing them at the point where it counts.

clue.text: ... "a twat essentially with too much capital" (6)

indicators.note: The essence of a word is what survives when the outside is stripped away, so only the middle letters are taken.

blocks.note: OTT is over the top, British shorthand for excessive
the word itself, taken in whole
the two letters at the centre of TWAT

explanation.surface: Somebody being written off as an idiot with far too much money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' is money in the insult and a city in the answer, and 'too much' is the British OTT rather than a quantity. The dots make this the end of a sentence begun two clues earlier.
explanation.definitionFit: Ottawa is the capital of Canada, the city on the Ontario bank of the river where the federal parliament sits.

clue.text: Stirring quality of playwright’s first swashbuckling role for 3 14A (6)

indicators.note: Whatever comes first in a word is the letter it begins with, and that is all this takes.

blocks.note: the letter that opens the word playwright
Athos is the senior of the three musketeers, played on screen by the actor named at 3 and 14 across

explanation.surface: The moving quality of the first swashbuckler a playwright wrote for one particular actor.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliver Reed played Athos in Richard Lester's The Three Musketeers, which is the role the cross-reference is pointing at. 'Stirring' is the emotional sense, nothing to do with a spoon.
explanation.definitionFit: Pathos is the quality in a scene that stirs pity in whoever is watching, so the definition names the effect rather than offering a synonym.

clue.text: Movie actors on vacation (8)

definitions.note: The definition names one particular film rather than films in general, and the grid runs the title's two words together.

blocks.note: the cast is the whole list of actors in a production
somebody on holiday is away

explanation.surface: A film's actors all off on holiday at the same time.
explanation.walkthrough: Cast Away is the film in which Tom Hanks is marooned on a Pacific island. Nothing in the clue marks the split, so the two pieces are read as one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Cast Away is a 2000 Robert Zemeckis picture, so the one-word definition is a title rather than a category.

clue.text: Island trips on hotel launch for Tom Cruise? (5)

definitions.note: The definition is the activity and the answer the vessel it is done in, a step the question mark owns up to.

indicators.note: Somebody who trips goes over, and in a down entry a word that goes over is read from the bottom up.
In a down entry one thing sits on another by resting on top of it, so these letters go above the letter named next.
The launch of a word is the letter it sets off with.

blocks.note: a cay is a low sandy island, the same word as the key in the Florida Keys, here turned upside down
H is hotel in the radio alphabet
the letter Tom sets off with

explanation.surface: Island excursions on the hotel's little motorboat, laid on for Tom Cruise.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface hands over Tom Cruise entire and the clue wants only the letter he starts with. 'Launch' looks like the hotel's boat and is the instruction to take that first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To cruise is to potter about on the water for pleasure, which is the one thing a yacht is built for.

clue.text: Fiddle with computers on the counter (4)

indicators.note: To run counter to a thing is to go the opposite way, so the word beside it is read backwards.

blocks.note: Macs are Apple's computers, written the other way round

explanation.surface: Messing about with the computers left out on the shop counter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiddle' is the swindle and not the violin, and 'counter' is the direction word rather than the shop fitting. Macs gives the plural the clue asks for.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiddle is British for a small-scale swindle - an expenses fiddle, a tax fiddle - which is what the answer names.

clue.text: Upset water swamps Tesla? (5)

indicators.note: To swamp a thing is to close over it completely, so the letters just named go right round what follows.

blocks.note: pee is the nursery word for the water the body passes
a Tesla is an electric vehicle, EV in the motor trade's shorthand

explanation.surface: Floodwater rising over a parked Tesla.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Water' is the lavatory sense, which is where the rudeness of the picture comes from. A Tesla is one EV among many now, which is what the question mark admits.
explanation.definitionFit: To peeve someone is to annoy them enough for it to show, which is the everyday sense of upset.

clue.text: Bold cycling competitor breaks hip (9)

indicators.note: Letters that cycle stay in the same ring and start from a different point, the ones at the front going round to the back.
Something that breaks a word splits it apart and settles into the gap.

blocks.note: chic is hip in the fashionable sense
a rival is a competitor, wheeled round so that the first two letters come off the front and go to the back

explanation.surface: A racing cyclist coming off and breaking a hip.
explanation.walkthrough: The cycling is a bike race on the surface and a letter-wheel underneath, and the hip stays a bone until the answer makes it fashion.
explanation.definitionFit: Chivalric conduct is the knight's: bold in the face of danger and courteous with it, which is how the word is used of anyone brave.

clue.text: Ready to shed one's last tear (3)

indicators.note: To shed a thing is to let it drop, so the letter named goes.
The last of a word is the letter it ends with.

blocks.note: fruit that is ripe is ready to eat
the final letter of the word one

explanation.surface: Somebody about to cry their very last tear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' is the trap: it wants to be the adjective the sentence needs and it is the ripeness of fruit. The last three words do two jobs, naming the letter to drop and then the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To rip a sheet is to tear it, the same verb in a blunter word.

clue.text: Private corporation with love for United (5)

indicators.note: Love is the nothing of the tennis score, written O, and United shortens to U on a football table, so putting the one in for the other swaps those letters.

blocks.note: a corporation is the old British word for a well-fed paunch

explanation.surface: A private firm with a soft spot for Manchester United.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' is the Victorian word for a belly, and the business sense is the decoy. The British private soldier took his nickname from the specimen pay book made out to Thomas Atkins.
explanation.definitionFit: Tommy is the affectionate name for the ordinary British soldier, the private in the ranks rather than anyone with a commission.

clue.text: Holding dog off its lead (5)

indicators.note: Something taken off a word is gone from it altogether.
The lead of a word is the letter out in front, the one leading the rest.

blocks.note: a basset is the short-legged hound with the trailing ears
the letter at the front of the dog's name

explanation.surface: Hanging on to a dog that has slipped its lead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' is the dog's on the surface and the word's first letter underneath, and 'off' does the removing. A basset is the low-slung hound bred for following a scent.
explanation.definitionFit: A holding is something you own and count towards your wealth, which is what an asset is on a balance sheet.
